claim: Sleep is present in animals as evolutionarily distant as Cassiopea jellyfish and the Australian dragon lizard.
source: Sleep is a widely expressed behavior, present in animals as evolutionarily distant as Cassiopea jellyfish and the Australian dragon lizard (Nath et al., 2017; Shein-Idelson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Nath et al., 2017; Shein-Idelson et al., 2016).

claim: Sleep disruption can perturb learning and memory consolidation.
source: Sleep disruption can perturb learning and memory consolidation (Walker and Stickgold, 2004; Krause et al., 2017), presumably through the modulation of synaptic plasticity (Frank and Cantera, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Walker and Stickgold, 2004; Krause et al., 2017).

claim: Sleep disruption presumably perturbs learning and memory consolidation through the modulation of synaptic plasticity.
source: Sleep disruption can perturb learning and memory consolidation (Walker and Stickgold, 2004; Krause et al., 2017), presumably through the modulation of synaptic plasticity (Frank and Cantera, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Frank and Cantera, 2014) and involves speculative reasoning ('presumably').

claim: Researchers have proposed that sleep stabilizes synapses.
source: Researchers have variously proposed that sleep stabilizes, strengthens, weakens, or even prunes synapses (Kavanau, 1996; Datta et al., 2008; Chauvette et al., 2012; de Vivo et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Researchers have proposed that sleep strengthens synapses.
source: Researchers have variously proposed that sleep stabilizes, strengthens, weakens, or even prunes synapses (Kavanau, 1996; Datta et al., 2008; Chauvette et al., 2012; de Vivo et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Researchers have proposed that sleep weakens synapses.
source: Researchers have variously proposed that sleep stabilizes, strengthens, weakens, or even prunes synapses (Kavanau, 1996; Datta et al., 2008; Chauvette et al., 2012; de Vivo et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Researchers have proposed that sleep prunes synapses.
source: Researchers have variously proposed that sleep stabilizes, strengthens, weakens, or even prunes synapses (Kavanau, 1996; Datta et al., 2008; Chauvette et al., 2012; de Vivo et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Miniature excitatory postsynaptic current amplitudes onto L4 and L2/3 pyramidal neurons were stable across sleep- and wake-dense epochs in primary visual cortex.
source: We found that miniature excitatory postsynaptic current amplitudes onto L4 and L2/3 pyramidal neurons were stable across sleep- and wake-dense epochs in both primary visual (V1) and prefrontal cortex (PFC).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (ex vivo measurements).

claim: Miniature excitatory postsynaptic current amplitudes onto L4 and L2/3 pyramidal neurons were stable across sleep- and wake-dense epochs in prefrontal cortex.
source: We found that miniature excitatory postsynaptic current amplitudes onto L4 and L2/3 pyramidal neurons were stable across sleep- and wake-dense epochs in both primary visual (V1) and prefrontal cortex (PFC).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (ex vivo measurements).

claim: Chronic monitoring of thalamocortical synaptic efficacy in V1 of freely behaving animals revealed stable responses across prolonged periods of natural sleep and wake.
source: Further, chronic monitoring of thalamocortical synaptic efficacy in V1 of freely behaving animals revealed stable responses across even prolonged periods of natural sleep and wake.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo optogenetic monitoring.

claim: Sleep does not drive widespread downscaling of synaptic strengths during the highly plastic critical period in juvenile animals.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that sleep does not drive widespread downscaling of synaptic strengths during the highly plastic critical period in juvenile animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript (mEPSC measurements and in vivo monitoring).

claim: The synaptic homeostasis hypothesis proposes that memories are formed during wake primarily through the induction of Hebbian LTP-like mechanisms that causes a net potentiation of synapses.
source: SHY proposes that memories are formed during wake when animals actively sample their environment, primarily through the induction of Hebbian LTP-like mechanisms that causes a net potentiation of synapses.
evidence: The claim describes a hypothesis from the literature (SHY) and is supported by citation context.

claim: The synaptic homeostasis hypothesis proposes that sleep is an offline state that allows neurons to renormalize synaptic weights by downscaling synaptic strengths.
source: This process would saturate synapses if left unopposed (Miller and MacKay, 1994; Abbott and Nelson, 2000; Turrigiano and Nelson, 2004), and sleep is proposed to be an offline state that allows neurons to renormalize synaptic weights by downscaling synaptic strengths (Tononi and Cirelli, 2014).
evidence: The claim describes a hypothesis from the literature (SHY) and is supported by citations.

claim: SHY predicts that excitatory synapses should on average be stronger after a period of wake, and weaker after a period of sleep.
source: Critically, SHY predicts that excitatory synapses should on average be stronger after a period of wake, and weaker after a period of sleep.
evidence: The claim describes a prediction from the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis and is based on established knowledge of the hypothesis.

claim: Slow wave activity is high during NREM immediately after prolonged wake and progressively decreases as sleep pressure diminishes.
source: It is well established that SWA is high during NREM immediately after prolonged wake and progressively decreases as sleep pressure diminishes (Dijk, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Dijk, 2009) and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: SHY proposes that the size of slow waves is correlated with cortical synaptic strengths.
source: SHY additionally proposes that the size of slow waves is correlated with cortical synaptic strengths, and that the oscillation in SWA with sleep and wake is driven by sleep-dependent synaptic downscaling that then diminishes SWA (Tononi and Cirelli, 2014; Tononi, 2009).
evidence: The claim describes a proposal from the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis and is supported by citations.

claim: The expression of proteins associated with synaptic potentiation are higher after a period of wake.
source: Studies supporting SHY have found that the expression of proteins associated with synaptic potentiation are higher, axon-spine interfaces (a corollary of synaptic strength) are larger, and evoked transcallosal cortical responses increase in slope after a period of wake (Vyazovskiy et al., 2008; de Vivo et al., 2017; de Vivo et al., 2019; Diering et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Axon-spine interfaces are larger after a period of wake.
source: Studies supporting SHY have found that the expression of proteins associated with synaptic potentiation are higher, axon-spine interfaces (a corollary of synaptic strength) are larger, and evoked transcallosal cortical responses increase in slope after a period of wake (Vyazovskiy et al., 2008; de Vivo et al., 2017; de Vivo et al., 2019; Diering et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Evoked transcallosal cortical responses increase in slope after a period of wake.
source: Studies supporting SHY have found that the expression of proteins associated with synaptic potentiation are higher, axon-spine interfaces (a corollary of synaptic strength) are larger, and evoked transcallosal cortical responses increase in slope after a period of wake (Vyazovskiy et al., 2008; de Vivo et al., 2017; de Vivo et al., 2019; Diering et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Other studies have found that synaptic transmission is potentiated by sleep.
source: In contrast, other recent studies have found that synaptic transmission is potentiated by sleep (Chauvette et al., 2012) or is unaffected by sleep deprivation (Matsumoto et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Chauvette et al., 2012).

claim: Other studies have found that synaptic transmission is unaffected by sleep deprivation.
source: In contrast, other recent studies have found that synaptic transmission is potentiated by sleep (Chauvette et al., 2012) or is unaffected by sleep deprivation (Matsumoto et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Matsumoto et al., 2020).

claim: Some studies have found oscillations in firing rate of individual neurons across sleep and wake states.
source: If excitatory synapses indeed oscillate in strength across sleep and wake states, then the firing rate of individual neurons would be expected to oscillate as well; while some studies have found such oscillations (but with variable effects between brain regions and neuronal populations; Vyazovskiy et al., 2009; Miyawaki and Diba, 2016; Miyawaki et al., 2019; Watson et al., 2016), others have observed stable firing across periods of sleep and wake (Hengen et al., 2016; Torrado Pacheco et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Some studies have observed stable firing across periods of sleep and wake.
source: If excitatory synapses indeed oscillate in strength across sleep and wake states, then the firing rate of individual neurons would be expected to oscillate as well; while some studies have found such oscillations (but with variable effects between brain regions and neuronal populations; Vyazovskiy et al., 2009; Miyawaki and Diba, 2016; Miyawaki et al., 2019; Watson et al., 2016), others have observed stable firing across periods of sleep and wake (Hengen et al., 2016; Torrado Pacheco et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hengen et al., 2016; Torrado Pacheco et al., 2021).

claim: Juvenile rats (postnatal days 25-31) were used to allow for high-quality endpoint slice recordings.
source: Here and in subsequent experiments, we used juvenile rats (postnatal days 25–31) to allow for high-quality endpoint slice recordings, and to ensure that our experiments were performed within a highly plastic developmental window when Hebbian and homeostatic plasticity are known to be pronounced (Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013; Hengen et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2009; Espinosa and Stryker, 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on methodological reasoning and established knowledge about slice recording quality.

claim: Postnatal days 25-31 in rats is within a highly plastic developmental window when Hebbian and homeostatic plasticity are known to be pronounced.
source: Here and in subsequent experiments, we used juvenile rats (postnatal days 25–31) to allow for high-quality endpoint slice recordings, and to ensure that our experiments were performed within a highly plastic developmental window when Hebbian and homeostatic plasticity are known to be pronounced (Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013; Hengen et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2009; Espinosa and Stryker, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Animals on average slept more during the light phase (~60% asleep) than during the dark phase (~40% asleep).
source: As expected, animals on average slept more during the light phase (ZT 0–12, ~60% asleep) than during the dark phase (ZT 12–24, ~40% asleep, Figure 1B,D; Frank and Heller, 1997; Frank et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,D and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: There was considerable variability from day to day and animal to animal in when they experienced periods enriched in sleep or wake.
source: however, there was considerable variability from day to day and animal to animal in when they experienced periods enriched in sleep or wake (defined as a 4 hr period with >65% of time in that state, Figure 1A, compare animals 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A comparing different animals.

claim: The average power in the delta band rose as net time spent awake accumulated in the dark.
source: As expected, the average power in the delta band (0.5–4 Hz), a proxy for slow wave amplitude (Dijk, 2009; Vyazovskiy et al., 2008), rose as net time spent awake accumulated in the dark (Figure 1C), and dropped during the day when animals typically spent more time sleeping (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Delta power dropped during the day when animals typically spent more time sleeping.
source: As expected, the average power in the delta band (0.5–4 Hz), a proxy for slow wave amplitude (Dijk, 2009; Vyazovskiy et al., 2008), rose as net time spent awake accumulated in the dark (Figure 1C), and dropped during the day when animals typically spent more time sleeping (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Changes in delta power over ZT in juvenile rats are similar to those seen in adult rodents.
source: These changes in delta power over ZT are similar to those seen in adult rodents (Leemburg et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to cited literature (Leemburg et al., 2010).

claim: The real-time classifier could determine the sleep/wake state of the animal with an accuracy of 93.3% when benchmarked against manual coding.
source: With this technique, we could determine the sleep/wake state of the animal with an accuracy of 93.3% when benchmarked against manual coding (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D comparing automated and manual classification.

claim: The average density of sleep epochs that exceeded threshold and were included in the mEPSC analysis was 69%.
source: The average density of sleep epochs that exceeded threshold and were included in the mEPSC analysis was 69%; the average wake density during the light period was 76% and during the dark period was 71%.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The average wake density during the light period was 76%.
source: The average density of sleep epochs that exceeded threshold and were included in the mEPSC analysis was 69%; the average wake density during the light period was 76% and during the dark period was 71%.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The average wake density during the dark period was 71%.
source: The average density of sleep epochs that exceeded threshold and were included in the mEPSC analysis was 69%; the average wake density during the light period was 76% and during the dark period was 71%.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: NREM bouts were more consolidated (longer) in the sleep-dense epoch as compared to wake.
source: NREM bouts were also more consolidated (longer) in the sleep-dense epoch as compared to wake (sleep 161.53 ± 10.4 s; light period, wake 120.97 ± 7.8 s; dark period, wake 122.16 ± 9.6 s; mean ± SEM).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing NREM bout durations.

claim: Mean mEPSC amplitude was stable across sleep- and wake-dense epochs in L2/3 pyramidal neurons of V1.
source: When we computed the mean mEPSC amplitude by cell and compared this across conditions, we found no differences in amplitude after sleep-dense or wake-dense epochs in the light phase (sleep and L. wake), or wake-dense epochs in the dark period (D. wake; Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There were no significant differences in the mEPSC amplitude distribution between conditions in L2/3 pyramidal neurons of V1.
source: To examine more closely the mEPSC amplitude distribution in the different conditions, we randomly selected the same number of events from each neuron and plotted individual mEPSC amplitudes as a cumulative distribution (Figure 3E, right). There were no significant differences in the amplitude distribution between conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: mEPSC amplitudes onto L4 pyramidal neurons in V1 were indistinguishable after wake-dense or sleep-dense epochs.
source: Similar to our observations in L2/3, mEPSC amplitudes were indistinguishable after wake-dense or sleep-dense epochs, and there was no difference in the cumulative amplitude distribution between conditions (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Mean mEPSC amplitude was stable across sleep- and wake-dense epochs in L2/3 pyramidal neurons of PFC.
source: However, consistent with our findings in V1, mean mEPSC amplitude was also stable across sleep- and wake-dense epochs in PFC and was not significantly different after extended wake at opposite circadian periods (Figure 3G, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: There was a small but significant rightward shift at the high end of the mEPSC amplitude distribution in PFC L2/3 neurons in the D. wake condition compared to sleep dense.
source: The cumulative amplitude distributions following extended sleep or wake in the light phase were indistinguishable (Figure 3G, right), but interestingly there was a small but significant rightward shift at the high end of this distribution in the D. wake condition (SD − D. wake, p=0.015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a small circadian modulation of mEPSC amplitude onto L2/3 pyramidal neurons in PFC.
source: This suggests that there is a small circadian modulation of mEPSC amplitude onto L2/3 pyramidal neurons in PFC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing differences between light and dark wake conditions.

claim: There were no significant differences in mean mEPSC frequency across any of the conditions or brain regions examined.
source: We found no significant differences in mean mEPSC frequency across any of the conditions or brain regions examined here (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Inter-event intervals were not different between conditions in visual cortex L2/3.
source: Inter-event intervals were not different between conditions in visual cortex L2/3 or L4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: Inter-event intervals were not different between conditions in visual cortex L4.
source: Inter-event intervals were not different between conditions in visual cortex L2/3 or L4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: In PFC, inter-event intervals were shorter in L. wake compared to both D. wake and L. sleep.
source: In PFC inter-event intervals were shorter in L. wake compared to both D. wake and L. sleep; thus there may be some interaction between time of day and sleep/wake state on mEPSC frequency in PFC, which does not generalize to visual cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: There may be some interaction between time of day and sleep/wake state on mEPSC frequency in PFC.
source: In PFC inter-event intervals were shorter in L. wake compared to both D. wake and L. sleep; thus there may be some interaction between time of day and sleep/wake state on mEPSC frequency in PFC, which does not generalize to visual cortex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing differences in inter-event intervals.

claim: There was no significant correlation between wake density and mEPSC amplitude.
source: There was a reasonable range of wake densities (from 65% to 90%) within the wake-dense condition, which allowed us to evaluate possible correlations between wake density and amplitude or frequency of mEPSCs; neither of these were significantly correlated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no significant correlation between wake density and mEPSC frequency.
source: There was a reasonable range of wake densities (from 65% to 90%) within the wake-dense condition, which allowed us to evaluate possible correlations between wake density and amplitude or frequency of mEPSCs; neither of these were significantly correlated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no relationship between the decrease in delta power during prior sleep and endpoint mEPSC amplitude.
source: However, when we plotted the decrease in delta power during prior sleep against the endpoint mEPSC amplitude or frequency, we again found no relationship (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: There was no relationship between the decrease in delta power during prior sleep and endpoint mEPSC frequency.
source: However, when we plotted the decrease in delta power during prior sleep against the endpoint mEPSC amplitude or frequency, we again found no relationship (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Postsynaptic strength in a range of excitatory neocortical cell types is remarkably stable across prolonged periods of sleep or wake.
source: Together, our data show that postsynaptic strength in a range of excitatory neocortical cell types is remarkably stable across prolonged periods of sleep or wake.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from mEPSC measurements across multiple cell types and brain regions.

claim: The amplitude of the first negative trough of the evoked response has the shortest latency in L4.
source: The amplitude of the first negative trough of this evoked response has the shortest latency in L4 (Figure 5B–D), where it arises primarily from monosynaptic thalamic excitatory synapses onto L4 neurons (Khibnik et al., 2010; Cooke and Bear, 2010), and thus represents an evoked field excitatory postsynaptic potential (fEPSP).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: The first negative trough of the evoked response in L4 arises primarily from monosynaptic thalamic excitatory synapses onto L4 neurons.
source: The amplitude of the first negative trough of this evoked response has the shortest latency in L4 (Figure 5B–D), where it arises primarily from monosynaptic thalamic excitatory synapses onto L4 neurons (Khibnik et al., 2010; Cooke and Bear, 2010), and thus represents an evoked field excitatory postsynaptic potential (fEPSP).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Khibnik et al., 2010; Cooke and Bear, 2010).

claim: fEPSP amplitude was rapidly modulated by behavioral states.
source: An interesting feature of these recordings is that fEPSP amplitude was rapidly modulated by behavioral states (Figure 5E,F), as previously reported (Vyazovskiy et al., 2008; Matsumoto et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Evoked fEPSPs were largest on average during NREM.
source: We found that evoked fEPSPs were largest on average during NREM, of similar size during quiet wake and REM, and smallest during active wake (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Evoked fEPSPs were of similar size during quiet wake and REM.
source: We found that evoked fEPSPs were largest on average during NREM, of similar size during quiet wake and REM, and smallest during active wake (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Evoked fEPSPs were smallest during active wake.
source: We found that evoked fEPSPs were largest on average during NREM, of similar size during quiet wake and REM, and smallest during active wake (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Changes in fEPSP amplitude manifested rapidly upon transitions between states.
source: These changes in fEPSP amplitude manifested rapidly upon transitions between states (Figure 5E), consistent with a rapid neuromodulatory effect (Lee and Dan, 2012; Brown et al., 2012; Matsumoto et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: fEPSPs were of consistently higher amplitude in all behavioral states in the light than in the dark.
source: A second feature of these fEPSPs is that they were of consistently higher amplitude in all behavioral states in the light than in the dark; there were no obvious circadian oscillations beyond a rapid change in amplitude at the transitions between light and dark periods (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: There were no obvious circadian oscillations in fEPSP amplitude beyond a rapid change at the transitions between light and dark periods.
source: A second feature of these fEPSPs is that they were of consistently higher amplitude in all behavioral states in the light than in the dark; there were no obvious circadian oscillations beyond a rapid change in amplitude at the transitions between light and dark periods (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: There were no progressive changes in fEPSP amplitude during prolonged sleep.
source: Strikingly, we saw no progressive changes in fEPSP amplitude during prolonged sleep (Figure 6B,C) or wake (Figure 6D,E) using either density threshold, even for the longest duration epochs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: There were no progressive changes in fEPSP amplitude during prolonged wake.
source: Strikingly, we saw no progressive changes in fEPSP amplitude during prolonged sleep (Figure 6B,C) or wake (Figure 6D,E) using either density threshold, even for the longest duration epochs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: fEPSP slopes did not change across sleep and wake states.
source: As fEPSP amplitude estimates can be contaminated by polysynaptic or spiking activity occurring after the evoked monosynaptic thalamocortical synaptic potentials, we repeated this analysis using a second standard measure of fEPSP magnitude, the slope of the initial downward deflection. Consistent with the amplitude measurements, the slopes did not change across sleep and wake states (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: fEPSP amplitudes were largely stable across periods of sleep or wake using the sandwich approach.
source: Using this sandwich approach, we again found that fEPSP amplitudes were largely stable across periods of sleep or wake (Figure 7B,C; <2% change), indicating that the intervening periods of sleep and wake produce no persistent change in synaptic strength.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: There was no significant correlation between epoch duration and change in fEPSP amplitude.
source: When we plotted the change in fEPSP amplitude against the duration of the intervening sleep or wake epoch, we found no significant correlation between epoch duration and change in fEPSP amplitude (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: Synaptic efficacy onto L4 excitatory neurons is stable across extended periods of sleep and wake.
source: Taken together with our mEPSC data, these experiments show that synaptic efficacy onto L4 excitatory neurons is stable across extended periods of sleep and wake.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from both mEPSC and fEPSP measurements.

claim: There were more evoked spikes on average during NREM than during REM or wake.
source: Consistent with the rapid brain-state modulation of fEPSP amplitude, there were more evoked spikes on average during NREM, an intermediate number during REM, and fewer during wake (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: There were no significant differences in evoked spiking before and after sleep- or wake-dense epochs.
source: We averaged the response for each isolated unit across all sleep- or wake-dense epochs (defined as >30 min periods when the animal was >75% asleep/awake), and found no significant differences in evoked spiking (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the length of a sleep/wake epoch and the change in number of evoked spikes.
source: Next, we took advantage of the variation in epoch durations to look for a correlation between the length of an epoch and the change in number of evoked spikes. We plotted the change in evoked spikes for each unit for each epoch, and found no significant correlation between duration of a sleep/wake epoch and ability of the thalamocortical stimulation to elicit spikes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: Time spent asleep or awake does not cause progressive changes in the efficacy of thalamocortical synaptic transmission in vivo.
source: Taken in concert with the fEPSP results, this shows that time spent asleep or awake does not cause progressive changes in the efficacy of thalamocortical synaptic transmission in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from both fEPSP and evoked spiking measurements.

claim: The real-time sleep classification approach allowed control for considerable variability across individual animals in sleep habits.
source: First, we carefully classified the sleep history of every animal used for our ex vivo recordings, which allowed us to control for the considerable variability across individual animals in sleep habits.
evidence: The claim is based on the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: In young animals (4-5 weeks of age), the average chance of having experienced a sleep-dense epoch at ZT 4 or 6 is <50%.
source: In the young animals studied here (4–5 weeks of age), the average chance of having experienced a sleep-dense epoch at ZT 4 or 6 (time points used in many studies) is <50%; our approach allowed us to wait until a sleep- or wake-dense epoch was detected within a specified circadian window for each animal to ensure consistency in sleep history.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis from the study.

claim: mEPSC measurements can reliably detect both increases and decreases of <10% in amplitude with a similar sample size to the present study.
source: We have used a similar approach to successfully quantify changes in mEPSC amplitude induced by visual deprivation and eye reopening, and can reliably detect both increases and decreases of <10% with a similar sample size to the present study (Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013; Hengen et al., 2016; Torrado Pacheco et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Previously reported changes in synaptic parameters following sleep or sleep deprivation are larger than 10%.
source: Previously reported changes in synaptic parameters following sleep or sleep deprivation are larger than that (de Vivo et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2010; Vyazovskiy et al., 2008), suggesting that if they were occurring at these synapses we would have been able to detect them.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Natural periods of sleep and wake do not by themselves globally modulate postsynaptic strengths.
source: Taken together, our data show that natural periods of sleep and wake do not by themselves globally modulate postsynaptic strengths.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from mEPSC measurements.

claim: Some studies have found learning-dependent changes in spine turnover during sleep.
source: The frequency of mEPSCs can be impacted by changes in the number of functional synaptic sites, but while some studies have found learning-dependent changes in spine turnover during sleep (Li et al., 2017), sleep does not constitutively drive changes in neocortical spine density (de Vivo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Li et al., 2017).

claim: Sleep does not constitutively drive changes in neocortical spine density.
source: The frequency of mEPSCs can be impacted by changes in the number of functional synaptic sites, but while some studies have found learning-dependent changes in spine turnover during sleep (Li et al., 2017), sleep does not constitutively drive changes in neocortical spine density (de Vivo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (de Vivo et al., 2017).

claim: One study found increased mEPSC frequency in frontal cortex after sleep deprivation.
source: Previous studies from PFC found inconsistent effects of sleep on mEPSC frequency; one study found increased mEPSC frequency after sleep deprivation (Liu et al., 2010) while another found no effect (Khlghatyan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Liu et al., 2010).

claim: One study found no effect of sleep deprivation on mEPSC frequency in PFC.
source: Previous studies from PFC found inconsistent effects of sleep on mEPSC frequency; one study found increased mEPSC frequency after sleep deprivation (Liu et al., 2010) while another found no effect (Khlghatyan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Khlghatyan et al., 2020).

claim: Sleep has been found to potentiate evoked responses in some studies.
source: Sleep and/or SWA has been variously found to potentiate evoked responses (Chauvette et al., 2012) or bias evoked responses toward depression (González-Rueda et al., 2018; Vyazovskiy et al., 2008), while a recent study using optogenetically evoked responses in mouse motor cortex found no impact of sleep deprivation on evoked transmission (Matsumoto et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Chauvette et al., 2012).

claim: Sleep has been found to bias evoked responses toward depression in some studies.
source: Sleep and/or SWA has been variously found to potentiate evoked responses (Chauvette et al., 2012) or bias evoked responses toward depression (González-Rueda et al., 2018; Vyazovskiy et al., 2008), while a recent study using optogenetically evoked responses in mouse motor cortex found no impact of sleep deprivation on evoked transmission (Matsumoto et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (González-Rueda et al., 2018; Vyazovskiy et al., 2008).

claim: A recent study found no impact of sleep deprivation on evoked transmission in mouse motor cortex.

claim: Some chronic long-term recordings have revealed an oscillation in frontal cortex firing rates consistent with changes in net excitatory drive.
